# Regional pricing — low and lower-middle-income markets

<!-- GENERATED by plan-iap-ppp.py (the shared iboalali-apps kit) — do not hand-edit. -->

**Live.** Every price below is what Play charges today — `prices.md` beside it agrees,
and there is nothing left to apply. Re-running the script is a no-op.

**56 of 172 regions** are priced from purchasing power across **6 products**.
Every other region, and every purchase made before the change, is untouched.

This is the product's **price** in each region, not a promotion on top of a higher one. Play's
promotional mechanism (an offer against a purchase option) is not used anywhere here: each
region carries a single price, so nobody is shown a struck-through "was" figure.

Those counts cover the regions Play prices. A further 0 are withdrawn, and 16 low and
lower-middle-income economies have no Play region at all — both groups are listed under
*Not sold in these markets*, so the numbers here are not read as reach.

## Why

Play's per-region prices were generated by converting one base price, so a region's price
tracks its *exchange rate* rather than its *purchasing power*. The lowest-income markets end
up paying about what the highest-income ones do:
India's INR 1300 is ~USD 13.49 at today's rate, against USD 11.99 in the United States — and the Indian figure is tax-inclusive where the American one is not, so the gap is narrower than it looks, but it still runs the wrong way.

So the World Bank's low-income and lower-middle-income economies are priced from purchasing
power instead, and every other region keeps the price Play generated.

## Method

A region's price is **its reference price times its tier factor**, rounded to a local price
point — not a fresh conversion from the anchor. The reference is the Play-generated price the
region carried before this policy applied, so it already holds Play's own exchange rate *and*
the region's tax treatment (India's figure includes 18% GST); scaling it preserves both, and
this repo never has to own an exchange rate or a tax table. References are pinned in
`ppp-reference-prices.json` rather than read from the live price, which is what makes the
script repeatable — scaling the live price would cut again on every run.

Price points are **.49 and .99** in the currencies Play quotes with decimals, and round numbers
in the ~35 it quotes in whole units (₹360, ₨880, KES 500 — the shape Play's own conversions
already take). Nothing lands on a third decimal: no price in this catalog uses one, and the
script refuses to build if one appears, rather than quantizing it away.

Factors are expressed against the anchor regions, read live from the snapshot so they cannot
go stale:

| Product | Germany (EUR) | USA (USD) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `tip_large` | EUR 11.99 | USD 11.99 |
| `tip_large_repeat` | EUR 11.99 | USD 11.99 |
| `tip_medium` | EUR 7.49 | USD 7.49 |
| `tip_medium_repeat` | EUR 7.49 | USD 7.49 |
| `tip_small` | EUR 2.99 | USD 2.99 |
| `tip_small_repeat` | EUR 2.99 | USD 2.99 |

Neither anchor is repriced — the script fails if an anchor region ever resolves into a tier.

| Tier | Factor | Regions | Effective | Basis |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Lower-middle income | 55% | 39 | 50%–60% | Moderate. World Bank lower-middle-income economies. |
| Low income | 20% | 17 | 16%–23% | Aggressive. World Bank low-income economies. |

Income bands come from `ppp-classification.json`, mirrored from the World Bank (GNI per
capita, Atlas method, 2025 unless a row says otherwise). The World Bank reissues
the classification every 1 July and countries do move between bands — Vietnam, the
Philippines, Indonesia and Sri Lanka have all left the lower-middle band this way. Re-run
`--refresh-classification` before a repricing and read the diff.

No price falls below the local equivalent of USD 0.49 (FX as of Sun, 04 Oct 2026 00:02:32 +0000), which is where Play's own minimum sits. The floor is
then snapped **up** to the nearest price point, so in a currency where it is not itself one
the effective minimum is slightly higher — the EUR-priced regions bottom out at EUR 0.99, about USD 1.11.
Snapping is what keeps the ladder intact: a floor sitting between two price points rounds the
cheaper product up and the dearer one down, squashing the very spread the lift protects.
Where that floor binds, the whole region is lifted by the same proportion rather than each
product being clamped on its own, so the products keep their usual spread instead of
collapsing onto the same price. That lifts those regions above their tier factor, which is what
the **Effective** column above reports.
The floor can only push a price up, and this plan never raises one: a region already cheaper
than the floor is left exactly as it is.

## Not sold in these markets

Neither group is a pricing decision, and neither appears in the counts above — listed so
those counts cannot be read as covering the income bands. They cover the regions Play
prices, which is not the same thing.

**No Play region configured — 16 economies** (8 lower-middle income, 8 low income). The policy
would reach these, but Play holds no price for them in any currency, so there is nothing
to price. 2 of them — Burundi, Afghanistan — are poorer than every region that *is* being cut (the poorest of those is $560).

## Syncing to Play

Read the diff first — between a product's snapshot and its proposal *is* the change:

```bash
cd "Play Store/In-App Products/pricing"
for id in tip_large tip_large_repeat tip_medium tip_medium_repeat tip_small tip_small_repeat; do
  git diff --no-index "$id.json" "proposed/$id.json"
done
```

Then dry-run and apply. `--regions-version` and `--update-mask` are both required, and
`--dry-run` is a *global* flag that goes before the subcommand:

```bash
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
for id in tip_large tip_large_repeat tip_medium tip_medium_repeat tip_small tip_small_repeat; do
  gplay --dry-run onetimeproducts patch \
    --package com.iboalali.basicrootchecker --product-id "$id" \
    --json @"Play Store/In-App Products/pricing/proposed/$id.json" \
    --regions-version 2026/01 --update-mask purchaseOptions
done
```

Drop `--dry-run` to apply, then reconcile:

```bash
fetch-iap-pricing.py     # snapshot catches up to the Console
plan-iap-ppp.py --check  # 0 pending changes once the two agree
```

Two things worth knowing before you run it. Price changes apply to **new purchases only** —
nobody who already owns a product is charged again. And Play keeps no price history and offers
no undo, so the pre-change snapshot in git is the only way back.
